text: The music for the Kingdom Hearts video game series was composed by Yoko Shimomura, with orchestral arrangements handled by Kaoru Wada. The original soundtracks have been released on three albums and a fourth compilation album. The series features musical pieces from both Square Enix and Disney, including "Mickey Mouse Club March" by Jimmie Dodd, "This Is Halloween" by Danny Elfman, and "One-Winged Angel" by Nobuo Uematsu, as well as well-known Disney film tracks such as "Winnie the Pooh" by Robert B. Sherman and Richard M. Sherman, "He's a Pirate" by Geoff Zanelli, Klaus Badelt, and Hans Zimmer, "Beauty and the Beast" by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, "Night on Bald Mountain" (rendered as "A Night on the Bare Mountain") by Modest Mussorgsky, and a remixed version of "One-Winged Angel" by Nobuo Uematsu. Several vocal songs are included, most notably the four main theme songs: "Hikari", "Passion", "Chikai", and "Face My Fears", with the two main themes written and performed by Japanese American pop star Hikaru Utada. The Japanese versions of "Hikari" and "Passion" are the theme songs for the Japanese releases of Kingdom Hearts and Kingdom Hearts II, respectively, while their English counterparts, "Simple and Clean" and "Sanctuary", are used for international releases and the Japanese re-release of the first game, Kingdom Hearts Final Mix. The songs share a similar melody but differ in lyrical meaning, with "Simple and Clean" not being a literal translation of "Hikari". "Hikari" was released in Japan on March 20, 2002, and sold over 270,000 copies in one week; "Simple and Clean" was included in Utada's single "Colors", which debuted at number one on Japan's Oricon charts and stayed for 19 weeks, and later appeared as a bonus track on Utada's 2009 English-language album This Is the One. Both songs have "PLANITb remix" versions and "Hikari" has a "Godson Mix", used at different points in the game. "Passion" was released on December 14, 2005, and "Sanctuary" was first previewed on MTV.com in early 2006; both the "Opening" and "After the Battle" versions of "Sanctuary" were released in May 2009 as bonus tracks on Utada's second American album, This Is the One. The "After the Battle" versions of "Passion" and "Sanctuary" serve as the ending theme songs for Kingdom Hearts 3D: Dream Drop Distance. The music ranges from dark to cheerful to sorrowful and includes original tracks such as the title screen track "Dearly Beloved", and the theme songs "Simple and Clean" and "Sanctuary". The main themes are pop songs, distinct from the rest of the music, which features a mix of piano and orchestral pieces. Kingdom Hearts II includes vocal songs like "Part of Your World" and "Under the Sea" from The Little Mermaid, composed by Alan Menken and Howard Ashman. Yoko Shimomura began composing video game music in 1988, joined Square in 1993, and left in 2002 to work freelance. She draws inspiration from travel and emotional experiences and respects solo and orchestral works such as Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 7, Chopin's Ballade No. 1, and Ravel's La Valse. She was initially hesitant to compose for Kingdom Hearts due to the mix of Square's narrative and Disney characters, but enjoyed arranging Disney themes and worked to preserve their original mood while adapting to the PlayStation 2's technical limitations, such as using a trial-and-error method for "This Is Halloween". She created original music to accompany gameplay and felt emotions like happiness and sadness in fight music, discussing ideas with director Tetsuya Nomura and game planners. For Kingdom Hearts coded, 358/2 Days, and Birth by Sleep, she composed the main themes while others handled the rest. She has stated that the series successfully combined scenes and music and feels honored that her music has resonated with fans. Hikaru Utada was chosen by Nomura as the only singer for the first theme song due to her ability to cross language and cultural barriers, and her involvement was announced in January 2002. Her participation in the sequel was announced in July 2005, and Nomura chose not to use a different singer for the second theme because fans associated Utada with the series. Utada drew inspiration from the game's worlds and characters and received story explanations from Nomura, who noted that the second theme tied more closely to the game's narrative than the first. The music has been released in various formats, with the first soundtrack released in Japan, the United States, and Europe on March 27, 2002 (Japan), November 25, 2002 (Europe), and March 23, 2003 (United States), and subsequent albums released only in Japan. The first soundtrack is a 2-CD set containing most of the original game's music, with bonus tracks, composed by Shimomura, vocals by Utada for "Simple and Clean" and "Hikari", and orchestral arrangements by Wada performed by the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra. The soundtrack was released after Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, so it does not include additional tracks from that version. The soundtrack received positive reviews, with IGN ranking "Dearly Beloved" as number four on their top ten RPG title tracks, being nominated for the "Best Sound in a PlayStation 2 Game Editor's Choice Award" and runner-up for the "Best Sound in Game 2002 Reader's Choice Award", and rated 3 out of 5 by Allmusic. GameSpy described it as "pleasant, melodious, and fitting for the various situations" and praised the English version of "Simple and Clean". The Kingdom Hearts Final Mix Additional Tracks CD, released in Japan on December 26, 2002, features new tracks from the re-release. The Kingdom Hearts II Original Soundtrack, released in Japan on January 25, 2006, contains music composed and produced by Shimomura, with orchestral arrangements by Wada performed by the Tokyo Philharmonic Orchestra and vocals by Utada for "Passion". It received positive critical reception, with G4TV awarding it "Best Soundtrack" at the 2006 G-Phoria awards, GameSpy noting it was not as strong as the first soundtrack, Game Informer calling it "unforgettable", and GameSpot praising it as a "superb soundtrack" and rating it 9 out of 10. The Kingdom Hearts Original Soundtrack Complete is a nine-disc compilation released in Japan on March 28, 2007, containing music from Kingdom Hearts, Chain of Memories, and Kingdom Hearts II, with unreleased tracks, new and rearranged versions from Final Mix releases and Re:Chain of Memories. It includes printed images on each disc and a deluxe booklet with illustrations by Tetsuya Nomura and comments from Shimomura, and a special CD case featuring Sora and Roxas artwork. Discs one and two contain unaltered tracks from the original soundtrack, discs three to six contain longer, looped tracks from Kingdom Hearts II, discs seven and eight contain tracks from Re:Chain of Memories, and disc nine contains bonus tracks from Final Mix versions. On May 27, 2009, Square Enix released a piano arrangement album of popular pieces selected by members of their music website, with a preview concert in Tokyo attended by lottery winners; Shimomura described it as consisting of easy listening piano solo arrangements, with tracks 5 through 8 forming a sonata on the series' themes. "The Other Promise" and "Roxas" are used in a cutscene of Kingdom Hearts Re:coded in Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 ReMIX, and the Piano Collections arrangement of "Dearly Beloved" appears in the title screen of Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 ReMIX, HD 2.5 ReMIX, HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, and HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX. Piano Collections Kingdom Hearts Field & Battle, released in Japan on January 13, 2010, features battle and world themes arranged by Sachiko Miyano and Natsumi Kameoka. Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep & 358/2 Days Original Soundtrack, released on February 2, 2011, features music from Birth by Sleep, 358/2 Days, and Re:coded, composed by Shimomura, Takeharu Ishimoto, and Tsuyoshi Sekito, with discs one and two containing music from Birth by Sleep and disc three containing music from 358/2 Days (tracks 1–13), Re:coded (tracks 14–20), and Birth by Sleep: Final Mix (tracks 21–27); the 358/2 Days and Re:coded tracks are in pure orchestrated form. Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance Original Soundtrack, released on April 18, 2012, includes tracks from The World Ends with You, remixed by Ishimoto, with orchestral arrangements by Wada. Kingdom Hearts 10th Anniversary Fan Selection: Melodies & Memories, released in Japan on September 19, 2012, features tracks chosen by fans from the official website. The music has been well received overall, with Greg Kasavin of GameSpot noting that the background music fits each setting but criticizing the loops as too short and repetitive, and IGN reviewer David Smith praising the production values, including the use of the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra and arrangements of "Night on Bald Mountain" and "Under the Sea", and highlighting Shimomura's ability to maintain atmosphere while creating a consistent musical thread.

Kingdom Hearts 10th Anniversary Fan Selection: Melodies & Memories is a 2-CD album released in Japan on September 19, 2012, to commemorate the series' 10th anniversary. The tracks were selected by fans through the series' official website. The music of Kingdom Hearts was generally well received; Greg Kasavin of GameSpot praised the background music for being appropriate to each setting but criticized the loops as too short and repetitive. IGN reviewer David Smith commended the production values, including the use of the New Japan Philharmonic Orchestra and arrangements of pieces like "Night on Bald Mountain" and "Under the Sea," and praised composer Yoko Shimomura for maintaining a consistent atmosphere with a unifying character thread throughout the soundtrack. Daniel Kalabakov of SoundtrackCentral.com described Shimomura's orchestral composition as "sophisticated" and noted the score's unique qualities, though he considered it one of her weaker albums overall. Adam Corn of SoundtrackCentral.com highlighted the Kingdom Hearts tracks as a standout on the compilation album Drammatica. Jim Cordeira of Gaming Age called the music one of the best aspects of the first game, noting the orchestrated soundtrack surpassed the "midi-sounding" tunes of earlier Final Fantasy titles. Benjamin Turner of GameSpy praised the main theme but found some world background music weak, while Gerald Villoria of GameSpy complimented both PlayStation 2 game soundtracks, stating that Kingdom Hearts II's soundtrack was not as strong as the first game's. Several tracks received special attention: "Hikari" debuted at number one on the Oricon Weekly Singles chart in Japan, remained at number one for three weeks, and stayed on the chart for thirteen weeks. It sold over 270,000 copies in its first week and surpassed 860,000 copies by August 2002, earning recognition from Guinness World Records in 2008 as the best-selling video game theme song in Japan. Kalabakov praised Utada's singing and instrumentation in "Hikari" but expressed a lack of preference for pop songs. Turner appreciated the English translation of "Hikari" and considered Utada's vocals a strong addition to the game's opening and ending segments. "Passion" debuted at number four on the Oricon Weekly Singles chart and remained on the chart for nine weeks. G4TV's Miguel Concepcion particularly liked "Dearly Beloved," the title screen track, which IGN also praised as number four on their top ten list of RPG title tracks, noting it lifted doubts about the game's potential. Kalabakov described "Dearly Beloved" as a fitting "fairy tale-style" piece with a simple yet emotionally rich composition.
